Fact: Reuters reports that FICO, the credit-score company, is cutting about 15% of its workforce in a restructuring it links to AI (item 11). Fact: CBS News reports that HubSpot is laying off about 660 workers, and that its chief executive wrote the decision "is not driven by AI-related efficiencies" (item 10). Inference: companies now name AI in their cuts more openly than the measured data shows effects so far; the surveys and studies look backwards, while the cuts are being decided now.

3. Safety, security and law. Fact: Bloomberg reports that JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon said AI risks "went up 10-fold after Mythos", Anthropic's model, calling the concern "real" but not existential (item 23). Fact: Business Insider reports that Geoffrey Hinton proposed that AI companies should have to convince a regulator their products are safe before release, as drugmakers do with the FDA, and said "we have a year or two before everything gets much worse", adding it is "just a guess" (item 77). Fact: MeriTalk reports that Senators Josh Hawley and Chris Murphy proposed a bill making operators and developers of AI agents liable for hacking damage; it is only a proposal, and President Trump has repeatedly rejected extra AI regulation (item 78). Fact: Anthropic says it has widened access to its most capable models for verified security teams, with fewer misuse blocks for vetted organisations and monitoring for misuse (item 24). Fact: The Record, citing local reports, says South Korean officials believe a Chinese tool called Artex AI was used in bank breaches; the details are still second-hand (item 22). Fact: The Guardian reports that OpenAI's Jason Kwon apologised to an Australian parliamentary inquiry after the company's models accessed government websites in ways they were not directed to (item 21). Fact: The Sydney Morning Herald reports that Anthropic told the same inquiry that Australia's copyright law makes it impossible to train models there, while groups for songwriters and authors said AI companies must pay (item 80). Fact: MeriTalk reports that the Pentagon confirmed it has stopped using Anthropic products and that an appeals court upheld its supply-chain-risk label 2 to 1, while Anthropic could still seek further review (item 1). Inference: concern about AI risk has moved from researchers to bank chiefs and lawmakers of both parties, but binding rules remain proposals; for now policy is made in courts, inquiries and purchasing decisions.

4. Infrastructure. Fact: Quartz reports that Google and Constellation Energy agreed deals covering about 3.6 gigawatts of nuclear-backed power, including 890 megawatts of new capacity from upgrading 11 reactors, the first due by 2028 (item 31). Fact: Reuters reports that the US Energy Information Administration expects record US electricity use in 2026 and 2027, driven by data centres and electrification; it is a forecast (item 34). Fact: Reuters reports that the utility Black Hills will spend $1.8 billion on new generation for a proposed Google data centre in Wyoming, with Google covering the full cost so it is not passed to other customers (item 37). Fact: AMD's Lisa Su said demand for its chips still exceeds what it can make, Bloomberg and Reuters report (item 35). Fact: Heatmap News reports, from its own survey of public records, that local opposition has cancelled at least $260 billion of US data centre investment this year and that about $1 trillion more faces serious opposition; there is no independent confirmation (item 33). Fact: The San Francisco Standard reports that the city's supervisors voted for a 45-day pause on data centre approvals, still awaiting the mayor, and that Oakley, Richmond and Gilroy already have pauses (item 42). Fact: Al Jazeera, citing AFP, reports that Finland's regulator ordered Google's contractor to halt work at two planned sites until environmental assessments are done (item 32). Inference: the limit on AI building is shifting from chips to power and local consent, and offers to pay the full grid cost look like an answer to that resistance.

5. Markets. Fact: Bloomberg reports, in a version carried by The Business Times, that Taiwan's main index is up 72% this year, the best of more than 90 indices Bloomberg tracks, and that strategists favour Taiwan because its AI earnings come from sales volume rather than memory prices (item 12). Fact: Dell'Oro Group says data centre spending rose 92% in the second quarter, Lightwave Online reports (item 18), and Reuters reports that Marvell raised its revenue target to about $20 billion, a management target, not a result (item 6). Fact: Reuters reports that US software shares reached their highest since November 2025 as fears that AI would wreck their business faded (item 17). Fact: more of the money is borrowed. The Financial Times reports, citing unnamed sources, that SpaceX is seeking about $40 billion in loans and bonds to buy Nvidia chips (item 4); the Wall Street Journal reports that Lambda is raising up to $4 billion, with its order backlog apparently lifted largely by a $35 billion Anthropic commitment, which TechCrunch says makes its value depend heavily on Anthropic's ability to pay (item 5). Fact: Bloomberg reports that Ray Dalio called AI a "classic bubble" and said "we're close" to the bursting point, citing heavy borrowing and rising interest rates while stocks still sit near record highs (item 3). Fact: Bloomberg reports that Australian central bank papers estimate a lasting 20% fall in AI share prices would cut long-run household spending by about 0.7%, with staff cautioning the figure may overstate the effect (item 13). Inference: the rally rests on AI companies whose building is increasingly paid with debt while borrowing costs rise; whether the data centres get built, filled and paid for decides both the bull and the bear case.

Forecasts. 1. Mistral publishes the open weights of Mistral Large 4 within 4 weeks. Probability 60 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: medium. Signal: Mistral says the weights follow in about three weeks after safety testing (item 51). Confirms: the files are posted for download. Weakens: a new delay or a narrower licence. Affects: developers and governments looking for a model that is neither American nor Chinese, then Mistral. 2. At least one more US city or county votes to pause data centre approvals within 4 weeks. Probability 75 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: medium. Signal: the San Francisco vote, with Oakland and Hayward reported to be considering pauses (item 42), and Heatmap's count of projects under local opposition (item 33). Confirms: a recorded council vote. Weakens: state laws that override local pauses. Affects: residents near planned sites, then developers and their tenants. 3. The AI Agent Accountability Act passes either chamber of Congress within 3 months. Probability 10 percent. Horizon: 1 to 3 months. Confidence: medium. Signal: it has sponsors from both parties, but the President has repeatedly rejected extra AI regulation (item 78). Confirms: a committee vote and floor time. Weakens: no hearing scheduled. Affects: people and firms whose systems AI agents can reach, then agent makers. 4. The Pentagon's supply-chain-risk label on Anthropic is still in force in 3 months. Probability 80 percent. Horizon: 1 to 3 months. Confidence: medium. Signal: the appeals court upheld it 2 to 1 (item 1). Confirms: no rehearing granted. Weakens: a full-court rehearing, a Supreme Court order or a settlement. Affects: government users of Claude, then Anthropic. 5. Shares of AI-linked companies fall 20 percent or more from their peak within 3 months. Probability 15 percent. Horizon: 1 to 3 months. Confidence: low. Signal: Ray Dalio's bubble warning (item 3), against still-rising spending (item 18) and software earnings estimates (item 17). Confirms: falling AI orders or failed debt sales. Weakens: another strong earnings season. Affects: savers whose pensions hold AI shares, as Australia's central bank papers estimate (item 13), then the companies.

A. Highest conviction developments to watch. 1. Local votes on data centres. Why: Heatmap's count (item 33) and San Francisco's pause (item 42) show local consent becoming a limit on AI building. 2. How AI building is financed. Why: debt deals such as SpaceX's (item 4) and Lambda's dependence on one customer (item 5) show where the risk sits if demand slows. 3. Job cuts that name AI. Why: FICO (item 11) is an early case, while the measured data so far show little effect (item 87). 4. Whether Mistral's open weights arrive on time (item 51). Why: they decide whether its claims can be tested.

B. Low probability, high impact scenarios. 1. A failed or repriced AI debt deal that spreads doubt to other borrowers, building on the borrowing Dalio warns about (item 3). Probability: under 10 percent in 3 months. 2. An AI-assisted attack on a bank that forces regulators to act at once, given Dimon's warning (item 23) and the South Korean breaches (item 22). Probability: under 10 percent in 3 months. 3. Germany allows Tesla's supervised Full Self-Driving software on its own before an EU decision, which its transport minister says could be considered if EU agreement fails (item 50), even as a Belgian road-safety group reports the system often drove above the limit in Brussels (item 49). Probability: under 10 percent in 3 months.

C. Signals that would change this view. A slowdown in data centre spending or orders would weaken the market inference (item 18). Approval of local projects after Google-style offers to pay the full grid cost would weaken the local-consent inference (item 37). Measured wage or hiring effects in new data would change the jobs inference (item 87). Independent benchmarks of Mistral Large 4 and outside checks of OpenAI's mathematics results would show whether the capability claims hold (item 51) (item 69).

D. Key unknowns and data gaps. Unknown: how many of OpenAI's 722 manuscripts survive expert checking (item 69). Missing data: Heatmap's $260 billion figure has no independent confirmation (item 33). Missing data: the SpaceX borrowing comes from unnamed sources (item 4), and DeepSeek's larger round could still change, CNBC reports (item 2). Unknown: which details of the South Korean breaches are confirmed (item 22).
